chapters.title: A Light on the Water
paragraphs: The lantern had been dark for twelve years, but tonight a seam of light cut through the fog as if the tower had remembered its own pulse.
Mara stood at the end of Pier Seven with her coat collar raised, watching the beam sweep over the moored trawlers and the broken clock on the fish market roof.
In this town, people trusted old stone before they trusted each other. If the lighthouse had spoken, someone had gone to great lengths to make sure she heard it.
She checked her notebook again: two missing ledger books, one anonymous postcard, and a key that smelled of salt and machine oil.
By the time the foghorn sounded, Mara knew she would not sleep. The light had called her by name.

chapters.title: Old Harbor Notes
paragraphs: The archive room in Harbor Hall was colder than the docks. Files were stacked in steel cabinets labeled with years no one wanted to revisit.
Mara found the lighthouse registry bound in green cloth and brittle tape. The page for winter storms had been cut cleanly from the spine.
She copied a sequence of tide marks into her notebook: 5.2, 4.8, 6.1. Beneath them was a phrase written in graphite: keepers lie in pairs.
When she looked up, the janitor was standing at the doorway with a ring of keys and a face that refused surprise.
He said only one thing before leaving: check the bell tower before sunrise.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Name
paragraphs: The bell tower steps spiraled upward in narrow circles. Dust rose with each footfall, and each footfall sounded like a second hand hitting glass.
On the landing beneath the bell, Mara found a brass plate with a name she had crossed out years ago in her own reports.
The name belonged to Jonas Keen, lighthouse keeper, presumed drowned. The brass was warm despite the morning cold.
Wedged into a crack behind the plate sat a folded map of the harbor with one buoy marked in red ink.
When the bell rang six times, the map slipped from her hand like it was trying to be read.

chapters.title: Sun before Storm
paragraphs: The first rule of dawn-song was simple: never sing the final note before the sun touched stone.
Arin had broken that rule once, and the village still carried the echo in cracked windows and restless sleep.
At the edge of the pass, she tightened the silk around her wrist and listened for the choir hidden in the wind.
Somewhere above the ridge, bells answered in a key no human throat could hold.
By noon, she would have to choose between silence and becoming the voice she feared.

chapters.title: The Broken Violin
paragraphs: The violin case had no handle, only scorched marks where one used to be.
Inside, the wood looked split beyond repair until Arin noticed the fractures moving like ink in water.
Each crack traced a path between songs she had never learned and names she did not remember speaking.
Master Vel warned her that instruments were doors pretending to be objects.
At dusk she placed the bow on the strings and felt the room hold its breath.
